title: Your younger self

segments.voice: Yesterday, family feuds, and Moses praying five words for the sister who spoke against him. Your line was one step. Today, someone you've known longer than anyone: the person you used to be.

An old notebook turns up in a box during a move. The handwriting is yours, but the person writing isn't quite. There's the plan to marry someone who turned out to be a disaster. There's the cruel joke about a friend. There's the decision that cost a job, or a year, or a relationship. Some people laugh at their old notebooks; some close them fast. Earlier this block was about forgiving yourself in general. Today is narrower: the younger one, who had less to work with. Two lines from the Bible can be read as speaking to that person.
screen: `AN OLD NOTEBOOK.` → `YOUR HANDWRITING, NOT QUITE YOU.` → `THE YOUNGER ONE.`

segments.voice: First, a stage, not a verdict. Paul, writing to the church at Corinth, says: "When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things." He doesn't say the child was wicked. He says the child understood as a child. The younger self had a smaller map, and acted inside it. Second, a prayer about youth. Psalm twenty-five asks: "Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my transgressions: according to thy mercy remember thou me for thy goodness' sake, O LORD." Two rememberings: don't remember the sins; do remember me. The psalmist isn't asking to be excused. He's asking to be seen as more than the worst of his younger days. Third, the trick of hindsight. Looking back, the warning signs are obvious, because now you know how it ended. Your younger self didn't. Blaming them for not knowing the ending is like shouting at a character in a movie you've already seen. Fourth, what the line is not. I didn't know then isn't the same as it didn't matter. If someone was hurt, amends still apply: make it right where you can. Forgiving your younger self doesn't cancel the repair. It sets down the blame, so the person you are now has the energy to do the repairing.
screen: `A CHILD UNDERSTANDS AS A CHILD.` · `REMEMBER NOT THE SINS. REMEMBER ME.` · `HINDSIGHT KNOWS THE ENDING.` · `FORGIVEN, AND STILL REPAIRING.` · then, large: `I DIDN'T KNOW THEN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a younger you, at a particular age, in a particular room: the clothes, the hair, the phone or the lack of one. Recall one thing that version of you did that still stings, then look at the person instead of the mistake: what did they know, what were they afraid of, who was teaching them? If it feels right, say your line silently to them, and if you pray, hold that younger self in your prayer.
Corinth. The church Paul wrote to, saying when he was a child he understood as a child, before he put away childish things. Today's word.
Your line: I didn't know then. Hindsight knows the ending; they didn't. Day nine hundred eighty-nine, done.

howItsDone: Jews and Christians pray the Psalms, including Psalm 25 with its request not to remember the sins of youth; Christians read Paul's line about childish things as part of his chapter on love, 1 Corinthians 13.

chat.says: Why go easy on who I was at nineteen? I made some awful choices.
options: You understood as a child then; set down the blame, and still repair what you can.
Because it didn't matter; young people's mistakes don't really count.
You shouldn't; replaying those choices is what keeps you from repeating them.
chat.meaning: Paul says the child understood as a child; the younger self had a smaller map. Setting down the blame doesn't cancel the repair.

Corinth.meaning: a Greek city whose church Paul wrote to

Paul.meaning: an early Christian teacher who wrote letters to churches

notes: Trapdoor third floor: in English (KJV) 'remember' appears twice in Psalm 25:7; the Hebrew uses the root zakhar in both places. Confirm before keeping 'one verb'.
Paul's line is about mature love in context (1 Corinthians 13); applying it to forgiving the younger self is a reading, framed as such.
